234.history: The Tuathaich mill-citadel on the north coast was Daniel Frayne's town. He had taught its children to fold a sheet and sew a book in his copying school, and when he died there as speaker of Tional nan Tuathach in {{year:VI-0020}} he was buried in the churchyard at the east end of the town, with a length of binding thread laid in his grave by the pupils who carried him. Tional nan Tuathach sent those pupils, the binders of Muileann leathan, to rebind its minute-books from the first meeting; they found the first book to be a harbour ledger of the humans' time with its old pages cut out close, and kept the stubs in the new binding. The rebound set was laid at Caol mhòr, and a second set, the minute says, was hidden elsewhere. The town kept its water-wheel turning for the grinding through the age though a factor of the south offered it an engine.
234.known_for: Daniel Frayne's grave and the binders of Tional nan Tuathach's books

354.history: The great mill on the river bend is Slighe a' Ghuail's yard, and the age changed it more than any town on the line. Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's first dubhan engine was hauled there on a wagon by twelve horses of Òrd Mhacha in {{year:VI-0022}}, a priest of the order standing in the ford to his thighs to speak them out of it and saying over the engine the blessing for a horse setting out on a long road. Eachann mac Ruairidh, of the yard families, learned to drive it and taught it to the others, the Frisealach brothers first; an old driver would not ride, a fireman was struck from the roll, and a boy of the yard rows was killed under a wagon in the first year. Two years later the coal engines were laid up, nine of them standing in the long siding with the grass coming up between the sleepers and the children of the rows playing at driving in their cabs. In the Board's own timetables the line lost the word coal from its name. In the war the yard went to a double shift and loaded sealed wagons of arms for Seann Bhral, signed for weight and not for goods; in the present year Eachann drove Slighe a' Ghuail's last run of coal.
354.known_for: Slighe a' Ghuail's yard and the first dubhan engine

492.history: The ford town on the east coast, under the pirate watch, sent its salt inland on the drove road past Baile ìseal behind oxen for as long as anyone remembered, until a salt-master of Àth bheag bought a dubhan lorry in the eighth year and sent the first salt west by it. The salt reached the yard at Muileann chrom and went on to Cathair dhearg in a covered wagon behind the empty tanks, the first load the new engine carried toward the capital that was not dubhan. The last ox-drove on the eastern salt road went the next spring, and within a few years the drovers of the east coast had sold their oxen. Its tinsmith made the iron hood for the trial lamp at Baile ìseal. In the war raiders from the eastern waters took two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burned a third while the fleets were in the north-west.
492.known_for: the eastern salt-road, and the first salt carried by lorry

395.history: The town of the great granary fields in the south was the drovers' country. In {{year:VI-0024}} the drover families of Achadh mhòr, with no oxen left to drive, sold their teams to farmers of the granary country at the drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às, and the works at the southern Seann Skell took the price of the beasts against eleven lorries. The inn kept its trade by selling the drovers dubhan. The harvest of the fields went down to the capital's mills by lorry in eleven days the next year, the old drovers watching it pass from the field-gates. Its granary factors sold oats to the western pit towns through Tional nan Tuathach in the years of the holdouts, and wrote to the Board that they knew of no rule against it. In the present year its harvest is the heaviest in a generation and the dearest to carry.

324.history: The harbour town of Am Buabhall Fortanach and its jugged buffalo kept both through the age. The pot wants a day's slow fire, and the inn put up its price by a third in the third year as the coal grew dear; the shipmasters ate it all the same. Its landlady Oighrig nic Iain did not hang her old taproom lamp over the door when the inns of the mining roads took dubhan, but set it, cleaned and empty, on the shelf above the till. The first lorry came down to the harbour in the ninth year, and its driver sold rides round the market square until the maor stopped him. The market-clerk of Doire shean kept the new count of the years and the old side by side in his book, and in the war a third column for the tithe. In the war A' chiad chabhlach's hulls lay in its harbour, a short walk from their station at Àth gharbh.
324.known_for: Am Buabhall Fortanach and its jugged buffalo

322.history: The small town of An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the old mining road kept its great inn through the age. The inn was rebuilt whole in the tenth year under a widowed landlady, who painted a new sign over her door naming what a traveller might buy there, beds and fire, and within the year half the great houses of the roads did the same. It filled to the stables at the end of the twentieth year with men walking to the drill hall at Cathair dhearg to hear their old companies' names read. In the present year it sells fuel at its yard, beds under its roof and suppers by a dubhan lamp, and its sign still names all three.
322.known_for: An Taigh-òsta Grianach and its sign of beds and fire

74.history: The town below An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road counted the coal going away in the carts that passed its inn: a third fewer in the third year, and its landlord shut one of his two stable yards. In {{year:VI-0031}} the Reòta was the last of the great inns to keep a wick lamp in every room, and its landlord wrote to the Board that he would go on doing so; the lorry-drivers who stopped there took their suppers by the fire. The enforcers' two lorries lay a night there on their way west. In the column's year the regiments' lorries took on fuel at a pump set up in its yard, the landlord renting the yard to the Board and keeping his wicks inside, and the last carter to bring coal down the north road carried a load for the Reòta's own kitchen and none for sale.
74.known_for: An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the last inn of the wick

418.history: The town below An Taigh-seinnse Mòr on the old coal road is known for its steamed carp. The inn's kitchen went back to steaming its fish over wood from the road's thorn hedges when the coal grew dear. In {{year:VI-0028}} the Mòr opened a second hall lit wholly by dubhan, let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the guilds, and the first wedding held in it was a carter's daughter of Cuan chrom's. In the twentieth year the carters of the north road talked in that hall through the autumn of regiments to be raised. In the present year the landlord hangs a dubhan lamp over his gate for the lorries that come by night.
418.known_for: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, its carp and its hall of dubhan light
